title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is not a failure of the camera system. The license plate readers did what they were built to do, and the person running the searches held valid access to them. The failure sits at the point of query, where an authorised operator can direct a surveillance network at a person for a reason unrelated to police work. The tool was used outside the conditions it was built for, by an insider rather than an outsider.

Catching it would have required oversight at the query layer rather than the credential layer. Access was granted by identity, so nothing in the system distinguished a search tied to an investigation from a search aimed at a private individual. Detection would have depended on reviewing query logs against case records, or on flagging repeated lookups of a person connected to the officer running them. The summary does not say whether any such audit existed.

What is not established: the headline and the summary give different counts of the searches, and the account rests on a certification order and a single outlet's reporting rather than a criminal finding. The summary records no verdict, and no motive beyond what the order attributes to Nygaard.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: In Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license plate readers 228 times from June to October 2023 to check where his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend were, according to a Kansas certification order. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted jealousy affected his actions. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
